```{r}
library(dplyr)

read_data <- \(f) read_csv(file.path("../cases/housing/data", f), show_col_types = FALSE)

subgroups <- read_data("display_subgroups.csv")

n_emails  <- nrow(read_data("housing_audit.csv"))

fmt <- \(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
pct <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(x, d), "%")
pe <- \(p) case_when(p < 0.0001 ~ "p < 0.0001", p < 0.001 ~ paste("p =", fmt(p, 4)),
                     .default = paste("p =", fmt(p, 3)))
num_word <- \(n) c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine",
                   "ten", "eleven", "twelve", "thirteen", "fourteen", "fifteen")[n]

n_spec <- nrow(curve)
n_neg_sig <- sum(curve$b_pp < 0 & curve$p < 0.05)
n_decisions <- n_distinct(menu$axis)
n_off <- sum(!menu$on_curve)
judged <- \(j) sum(menu$judgement == j)
variance <- anova(lm(b_pp ~ comparison + population + uncoded + model + adjust, data = curve))
var_share <- setNames(100 * variance$`Sum Sq` / sum(variance$`Sum Sq`), rownames(variance))
by_pop <- curve |> summarise(lo = min(b_pp), hi = max(b_pp), .by = population)
bp <- \(pop, col) by_pop[[col]][by_pop$population == pop]
no_evidence <- analysts |> filter(task1 == "no evidence either way") |> pull(id)

# The EU-frames case, for section 9; pct_eu() takes values already in per cent and
# rounds halves up, as the specification menu of that case does, so that the pages agree

forks <- read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>

cnames <- read_csv("../cases/eu-frames/data/display_country_means.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(cntry, country)

# fixed decimals and a true minus sign
num <- \(x, d = 3) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
pct_eu <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(floor(x * 10^d + 0.5) / 10^d, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
minus <- \(x) gsub("-", "−", format(x), fixed = TRUE)

# shares of a set of curve rows below zero, and below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05
below <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$supports)
below_sig <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$supports & d$sig)
fk <- \(ax, col = "share") forks[[col]][forks$axis == ax]
dv <- \(ax, op, col) devs[[col]][devs$axis == ax & devs$option == op & devs$rule == "wcr_rademacher"]
eu_ref <- eu_curve |> filter(is_reference)
twoway <- eu_curve |> filter(estimator == "fe_twoway")
country <- eu_curve |> filter(estimator == "fe_country")

# the displays of section 9.5: the reproduced specification and its country twin
is_ref_spec <- \(d) d$outcome == "mcosmo" & d$predictor == "unemp" & d$copredictor == "none" &
  d$pred_form == "raw"
per_ref <- \(smp, col) periods[[col]][is_ref_spec(periods) & periods$estimator == "fe_twoway" &
                                        periods$sample == smp]
per_unemp <- periods |> filter(predictor == "unemp")
loo_two <- loo |> filter(estimator == "fe_twoway", left_out != "none")
loo_cty <- loo |> filter(estimator == "fe_country", left_out != "none")
vs <- \(cc) loo_two$variation_share[loo_two$left_out == cc]
ba <- \(grp, col) bailout[[col]][bailout$outcome == "mcosmo" & bailout$predictor == "unemp" &

design_label <- c(fe_twoway = "Two-way fixed effects", fe_country = "Country fixed effects")
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) works on two cases: sections 1 to 8 use the housing-audit case, and section 9 the EU-frames case.

The module is about the method that the course teaches, the multiverse or specification curve: where the idea came from, what it is claimed to do, and the arguments that are now being made against it. The course has you run one. You fix a specification in a preregistration, fit it, and read your result against the `r n_spec` specifications of the curve of the claim on the [multiverse page](../cases/housing/multiverse.qmd). The claim, from a field experiment by the original authors (OAs) on emails to public housing authorities [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect], is that "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts". The method is under live debate in 2025–26, the objections to it are serious, and the aim of the module is that you can take a position in that debate. Throughout, the housing-audit case serves as the worked example, and it is an unusual one, because on this case every specification agrees and a replication with new data still failed.

## 1. Origins {#sec-origins}

The founding statement is a 2016 paper by Steegen, Tuerlinckx, Gelman and Vanpaemel [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse]. Their starting point is the construction of the data before any model is fitted: turning raw data into an analysable dataset involves choices – which cases to exclude, how to code a variable, where to cut a scale – and several options are usually reasonable. Instead of privileging one dataset, they propose building every dataset that a reasonable set of choices could have produced and running the analysis on all of them, so that the reader learns how much the conclusion owes to decisions that nobody would defend as the only right ones. The idea connects to the 'garden of forking paths' of @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience: a researcher who makes each choice once, on the fly, has walked one path through a branching garden, and the single p-value at the end keeps no record of the branches. The 2016 paper states its ambition plainly, that "it should become standard practice to go beyond a single data set analysis and to acknowledge the multiverse of statistical results", and concedes at once what the critics would later press, that "performing a multiverse analysis will often be difficult, and to a large extent subjective" [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, p. 710]. The authors also sketched the extension that a curve of models puts into practice, a *model* multiverse, in which "One specific analysis thus corresponds to a single sample from a model multiverse" [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, p. 710].

The multiverse of the original paper was *customised for critique*: the alternative datasets were choices that the original authors of the target study "might themselves have considered", drawn from their own prior publications. It was therefore a post-mortem on the flexibility of one team rather than a general survey of the ways in which the question could be answered, and the distinction matters again in section 2. Steegen and colleagues also place the idea in an older lineage that runs through perturbation and sensitivity analysis in economics and Bayesian statistics; what the 2016 paper added to that lineage was the demand that the whole distribution of results be shown.

The modelling side was developed separately as **specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis], which enumerates the defensible ways of specifying a test, estimates all of them, plots the estimates in order and, in its full form, tests the curve as a whole against a null distribution built by permutation, that is, by reshuffling the data so that any true effect is removed. The multiverse page of the course uses this display. A distinct strand kept the data and the question fixed and varied the *analysts*: 29 teams answering one question about football referees with odds ratios from 0.89 to 2.93 [@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne]; 73 teams testing one hypothesis about immigration and social policy, with more than 95% of the variance in their results left unexplained even after coding every identifiable decision in the workflow of every team [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]; and the Multi100 project, in which 457 reanalysts carried out 504 reanalyses of claims from 100 published studies [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. The housing-audit case is one of those hundred, and its five reanalysts are presented on the [case study](../cases/housing/index.qmd#sec-reanalysts). A further strand proposes Bayesian hierarchical models for aggregating such data [@HoogeveenEtAl2020ImprovingStatisticalAnalysis]. The course combines the strands: the curve of the claim is a model multiverse, and the five Multi100 analysts and the class chart are a many-analysts layer beside it, meant to be read against it.

## 2. Three purposes {#sec-purposes}

Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask the question that organises the current debate, which is what a multiverse is *for*. They distinguish three uses, "as a tool for reflection and critique, as a persuasive tool, as a serious inferential tool", and attach a failure to each: "it fails as a persuasive tool when researchers disagree about which variations should be included in the analysis", and "it fails as a serious inferential tool when the included analyses do not target a coherent estimand" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1]. Their conclusion is mild. The multiverse "does remain a valuable tool", but they "urge against taking it too seriously" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1].

The three purposes impose different rules for building the set of specifications. A multiverse built for critique may mix analyses that answer slightly different questions, since its aim is to show that researchers plausibly disagree about the question, and "it may be perfectly sensible to include analyses with different estimands as long as it is plausible that researchers may try out different estimands" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 6]. The same set cannot then be read as inference about one quantity. Hullman puts the condition in a companion blog post: "what kinds of equivalence are needed will also depend on your goal in using a multiverse" [@Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood].

The course builds its artefacts to different rules for that reason. The [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd) of `r num_word(n_decisions)` decisions, the [decision map](../cases/housing/map.qmd) and the class chart serve reflection, since they make visible how much a result depends on decisions that look arbitrary from outside, and they show options that answer other questions beside those that answer the claim. The curve of `r n_spec` is built to the standard that inference would require and is used to persuade: every specification on it is meant to answer the claim as the course reads it, and the two decisions that leave two estimands on it, the comparison group and the emails counted, are named as such. The EU-frames case applies the same rules to a menu of fourteen decisions, and section 9 reads its curve against the arguments of sections 3 to 6.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Assign each artefact of the course to one of the three purposes: the specification menu, the preregistration of Task 5, the curve of `r n_spec`, the randomisation test stored for each specification, and the class chart. For each, write one sentence on what the set of specifications would have to look like for that purpose to be served. Note where one set of analyses is being used for two purposes.
:::

## 3. The pruning critique {#sec-auspurg}

The most direct empirical disagreement in the recent literature is between a study of model uncertainty by Ganslmeier and Vlandas and the reply of Katrin Auspurg. Ganslmeier and Vlandas cross five dimensions of specification at once, across four literatures of political science, and produce about 3.6 billion estimates. They find that "the sign and statistical significance of estimates is more contingent on the underlying sample and the operationalization of indicators than on the inclusion of the control set" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 6], and they state the dilemma themselves: "Running all possible models risks introducing errors in the empirical approach, but selecting a subset of robustness checks risks reintroducing the 'researcher's degree of freedom'" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 2].

Auspurg replies that "Multiverse analyses are only informative when all included models represent equally plausible strategies for estimating the same estimand" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. Her charge is that their set is heterogeneous, in statistical quality and in what each model estimates, so that its distribution pools numbers that cannot be compared. She names four kinds of nonequivalence: statistically inferior models ("Many models do not include fixed effects or cluster-robust SE, which are standard in panel data analyses" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]); unstable country subsets; causal misspecification from randomly combined covariates; and measurement nonequivalence, where "Outcomes differ in scope … and are sometimes negatively correlated. This clearly indicates that they do not reflect the same construct" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. Restricting it to the 1,152 models that she classes as justified, against 91,008 unjustified ones, turns a 60/40 split among the significant coefficients into 97% pointing the same way. She rules out choosing models by their fit, noting that "Ironically, the authors' own fit criterion (AIC) consistently favors unjustified models" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1], and puts the remedy before estimation, in "thorough, theory-based model selection" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 2]. The constructive version of the same demand is the rule of estimand consistency in the book by Young and Cumberworth, under which "any 'necessary control' requires a clear causal diagram or definitional justification supported by prior research" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 57]. They are also explicit that "there is nothing in the distribution of estimates per se that tells us which is the true effect" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 119].

The course applied her test to its own menu. For every option of the `r num_word(n_decisions)` decisions, the course asked whether that option is a justifiable way of answering the claim as the course reads it. Of the `r nrow(menu)` options, `r judged("kept")` are on the curve and `r n_off` are not: `r judged("other_question")` answer another question, `r judged("weaker_answer")` answer this one less well, `r judged("check")` check an answer that the curve already holds, and `r judged("unavailable")` cannot be fitted on the public file. The options that answer another question are off the curve but stay in the course, and @tbl-off shows why they would not belong in a count of votes on the claim: each gives its own answer to its own question.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-off
#| tbl-cap: "Options that answer another question than the claim, with the result that each gives on the housing-audit data: a difference in percentage points against the white names, as a difference in proportions with an HC2 test. Sources: `cases/housing/data/display_outcomes.csv`, `cases/housing/data/display_subgroups.csv`."
row_out <- \(o, cn, label) outcomes |> filter(outcome == o, contrast == cn) |> mutate(Option = label)
row_sub <- \(start, label) subgroups |> filter(startsWith(subgroup, start)) |> mutate(Option = label)
bind_rows(
  row_out("reply", "hispanic", "Outcome: any reply"),
  row_out("reply24", "hispanic", "Outcome: reply within 24 hours"),
  row_out("named", "black", "Comparison: Black names, greeted by name"),
  row_sub("male", "Names: male names only"),
  row_sub("female", "Names: female names only"),
  row_sub("replies from officials", "Who replied: officials with Hispanic names")
) |>
  transmute(Option, `Gap (points)` = fmt(b_pp), p = pe(p), Emails = n) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(j = 2:4, align = "r")
```

On this case the pruning removes little that would change the picture of the claim itself. The options off the curve give answers to their own questions, some in the direction of the claim on fewer emails or with less precision, and one, the speed of replies, in the other direction. Counted as votes on the claim they would mix questions, and kept as displays they describe the experiment. The decisions that remain on the curve move the size of the gap, and none of them moves its sign.

## 4. One correct analysis {#sec-lakens}

Lakens, Rasti and Tunç push the criticism further. Their target is the inference that many people draw from analytic variability, that since reasonable analyses disagree, there is no single correct analysis and researchers should report distributions instead. They separate random variation, which standard errors quantify, from uncertainty about which auxiliary assumptions are true – which measure is valid, which units belong in the sample, which adjustment set is right – and argue that the second is reduced by doing research rather than absorbed by wider intervals. Once the auxiliary assumptions are fixed, "there is a fact of the matter about which analysis correctly implements that test" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 7], robustness "is a consequence of valid tests, and not a goal in itself" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 15], and "Variability across specifications based on uninformed hunches, especially when less plausible alternatives are included, provides little actionable insight" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 10].

Their argument applies most sharply to the decision that dominates the housing curve, which emails to count. The claim concerns the tone of the replies that came, which points to the comparison among replies, but that comparison is a pure effect of the name only if the name did not change who replied, an assumption that the data cannot test. On their view, an analyst should settle which question is being asked, and argue for the assumption that the chosen comparison needs, before the test, rather than report both and let the reader average them. The [causal-graphs module](dags.qmd#sec-case) sets out what each answer assumes.

It is tempting to answer them with Task 5, where you fix one specification before running it. The two devices solve different problems. Preregistration solves a problem of timing, since it rules out choosing a specification after seeing where the numbers fall, a real worry, because "in the absence of preregistration, researchers may as well determine what is equivalent based on whether or not it supports their result" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 5]. The argument of Lakens and colleagues is about warrant, which does not depend on timing, since an arbitrary choice stays arbitrary when it is preregistered. Two caveats cut against the device that the course itself uses. Preregistering a reanalysis of data that already exist is a weaker form of it, since "[w]hen the data already exist, authors can explore the data prior to registering their analysis" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 149]. And the two approaches can be combined: "one could preregister a multiverse analysis to combine the strengths of both approaches" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 9].

## 5. The decomposition of the curve {#sec-forks}

The variance of the `r n_spec` estimates can be split by decision, and on this curve the split is lopsided. The emails counted carry `r pct(var_share[["population"]])` of it, the comparison group `r pct(var_share[["comparison"]])`, the adjustment `r pct(var_share[["adjust"]])`, the uncoded replies `r pct(var_share[["uncoded"]])` and the model `r pct(var_share[["model"]])`, with `r pct(var_share[["Residuals"]])` left to the interactions between decisions. Among the replies the estimates run from `r fmt(bp("replies", "lo"))` to `r fmt(bp("replies", "hi"))` points, and among all delivered emails from `r fmt(bp("all", "lo"))` to `r fmt(bp("all", "hi"))`.

Numbers like these invite the reading that the spread of the curve is a spread of estimates of one quantity. The decision on which emails to count, however, is a fork of estimands. A gap among the replies and a gap among all delivered emails, with an email without a reply counting as no greeting, answer two related questions, and the curve names them as two estimands instead of presenting their distance as uncertainty about one. Read that way, the decomposition locates where the argument has to happen, a use that every party to the debate endorses. Lakens and colleagues "support the use of multimodel analyses to hypothesize about 'which analytical decisions are most consequential'" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 6], and Ganslmeier and Vlandas offer their method as something that "can help inform which combinations of choices are more or less warranted" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 6]. On this curve the decomposition says that one decision needs a theory, which emails to count, and that the choice of model or of covariates matters little.

## 6. Frequency and probability {#sec-reading}

One practical rule from the literature that criticises the method concerns how to *read* a curve, and it prohibits treating frequency as probability. The share of specifications that support the claim, here `r n_neg_sig` of `r n_spec` below zero with p < 0.05, describes a curated set of analyses, and it is not the probability that the claim is true. Rohrer and colleagues ask for variation to be "treated possibilistically", any result found anywhere in a justified set being a live possibility, and they attach a condition: "This possibilistic interpretation is only sensible if every universe included is indeed deemed justified" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 6]. The Milliways project shows how standard displays emphasise how *often* an outcome occurs and so invite "misleading, probabilistic conclusions" [@SarmaEtAl2024MilliwaysTamingMultiverses]. Lakens and colleagues put it most bluntly: "Scientists should not compute the percentage of agreement across different data-analytic strategies, because we do not resolve scientific disagreement by majority vote" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 16].

Rohrer and colleagues add that a multiverse persuades only under a precondition: "This can only work if the results are fairly unambiguous across specifications" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 3]. The housing curve meets it completely, since every specification points the same way and clears the 5% threshold by a wide margin, and section 7 asks what that settles about the claim.

The live class chart on the multiverse page, on which every submitted specification appears as a mark over the curve, is best read as a many-analysts demonstration, the classroom analogue of the 29 and the 73 teams, with the extra property that every declared specification was fixed in a preregistration before it was run. Heyman and Vanpaemel, who run multiverse projects with students, describe the design as "comparable to the many-analysts-one-dataset approach used by Silberzahn et al. (2018)", and note that when several analysts each make their own choices "there is a multiverse of multiverse analyses" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 7]. On this case the class will agree on the direction, and the interest lies in the sizes, and in whether the class, like the five Multi100 analysts, reads the same evidence as support for the claim or not. Two of the analysts, `r paste(no_evidence, collapse = " and ")`, concluded in the first task of Multi100 that the data showed no evidence either way: one judged the claim by the size of its gap, which the analyst found significant but smaller than the twenty points of the abstract, and the other by a test that compared the female names alone (p = 0.13), before a significant gap in the second task.

## 7. Robustness and replicability {#sec-replicability}

SCORE, the programme from which Multi100 came, put claims through three kinds of repetition [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. A reproduction repeats the original analysis on the original data, a robustness check applies different but defensible analyses to the same data, and a replication asks the same question of new data. A multiverse is a robustness check in that sense, however large it is. Every one of its specifications is fitted to the same `r format(n_emails, big.mark = ",")` emails, so that a chance feature of that sample, a run of unusually cold replies to Santiago in one week of 2014, would be found by every specification together. The specifications are not independent tests, and their agreement is evidence about the analysis, given the data.

The housing-audit case separates the two properties cleanly. On the original data all `r n_spec` specifications are negative and significant, from `r fmt(min(curve$b_pp))` to `r fmt(max(curve$b_pp))` points, and the randomisation test stored for each specification gives at most p = `r fmt(max(curve$p_ri), 4)`. The SCORE replication then emailed 3,050 housing authorities from new names, and its logistic coefficient for the Hispanic names was positive and far from significant (z = 0.66, p = 0.511). The curve could not have warned of this. Its specifications vary the analysis and hold the sample fixed, so their agreement says nothing about how far a new sample might differ, which is what the confidence interval of any one of them describes. The candidates for the difference lie outside the curve: the names, which conveyed more than ethnicity; the authorities and the year; and the power of the original comparison, which leaves a significant estimate from a study of its size likely to overstate the effect, as the [audit-experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-power) shows. Robustness to analytic choices and replicability are separate properties of a finding, and this case has the first without the second.

## 8. The multiverse in the classroom {#sec-teaching}

Every side of the debate agrees that the multiverse is useful in teaching. Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman concede that "the multiverse has been a valuable training tool" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 8], and Heyman and Vanpaemel build their teaching on it, with two rules that the course follows. The first puts the reasons before the number of paths: "the goal should not be to merely devise as many paths as possible", and "[t]he key is that the alternatives are properly motivated" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 4]. That is why every option of the menu carries a reason. The second is pastoral: "one should be cautious that students do not completely lose faith in (psychological) science" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 9]. A day that follows a published claim through every defensible analysis, only to learn that a new experiment found nothing, could leave a class cynical. The case can also be read the other way, as research working as it should: the data were public, five analysts and a class could check the claim, and a replication could test it.

Hullman gives a further reason why this literacy will matter more. Building a multiverse is becoming cheap, because "lots of forms of robustness checking that used to be difficult are now trivially easy" [@Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood] once software can generate the specifications. When anyone can produce a curve on demand, the skill that remains scarce lies in judging what belongs in it, naming the purpose that it serves, and refusing the readings that its construction cannot support.

## 9. The multiverse at scale: the EU-frames case {#sec-eu-frames}

The housing-audit curve is small and unanimous. The EU-frames case shows the same debate on a curve of `r nrow(eu_curve)` specifications, built from a menu of fourteen decisions, on which the strength of the evidence depends on the decisions. Its claim, from a paper of 2016 [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic], is that "poor national economic performances significantly decrease positive EU-framing dimensions". The subsections below read the arguments of sections 3 to 6 against that curve, and the last sets out the displays that the course keeps beside it. The section is a companion to [the inference reading](../cases/eu-frames/reading-inference.qmd) of the case, which covers one narrow question, namely what a test of the curve as a whole can and cannot establish.

### 9.1 Pruning a menu of fourteen decisions {#sec-eu-pruning}

The EU-frames case applied the test of Auspurg, and the stricter standard that Rohrer and colleagues set for a multiverse used for inference, to its own menu. Every option of every decision was asked one question, whether it is a justifiable way of answering the claim as the course reads it, and the options that failed left the curve without leaving the course. Three of her categories reappeared. The pooled estimator, fitted without country effects, falls in her first category, and so do the conventional standard errors of the fixed-effects designs, which treat the ten years of a country as independent although the residuals of a country correlate from one year to the next; the curve keeps the two fixed-effects designs and classes every point by a wild cluster bootstrap by country, as the [statistical methods module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-inference) explains. The four restricted samples, two periods and two sets of excluded countries, are versions of her second category, and the findings that they carry moved to the displays of section 9.5. Her fourth category, measurement nonequivalence, described the outcome axis of the full menu, on which six framing scales of different scope stood in for 'EU framing'.

The four scales of the paper are shares of one instrument that sum to one for each respondent who mentions anything, and the two composites are sums of them, so whatever raises one share must lower the others, and [the simulation module](simulation.qmd#sec-outcomes) lets you examine the arithmetic directly. Under the convention of the course panel, which scores a respondent who mentions nothing as zero, the cell means of the positive and the negative composites sum to one minus the share of silent respondents, so that a confirmation of the claim on the negative composite largely counts the result on the positive composite a second time. The communitarian scale also contains the item "unemployment", which ties the outcome to the predictor by content. The curve of the claim therefore keeps the three positive scales that the claim names, scored as shares, as the paper scores them, while the negative scales have a curve of their own as the other half of the first hypothesis of the paper, and the count of items, which measures how much a respondent says about the EU rather than how the EU is framed, is taught in the [items module](measurement.qmd).

@fig-off-curve shows what each option that left the curve does when it is swapped into every specification of the curve with everything else held as it was. The reason recorded for each, in the list of options that the specification menu draws on (`cases/eu-frames/data/menu_options.csv`), is one of three: the option answers another question, it answers this question less well because an assumption that it needs fails on these data, or it is a check of an answer that the curve already holds.

```{r}
#| label: fig-off-curve
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Options that left the curve of the claim, each swapped into the specifications of the curve to which it applies: the share of the refitted specifications that lie below zero with p < 0.05. The vertical line marks the curve itself (", pct_eu(below_sig(eu_curve)), "). Each option is tested under the rule that fits it: the wild cluster bootstrap for linear models fitted by least squares, errors clustered by country on 26 degrees of freedom for random effects, the beta family and the imputed variants, and CR2 for the within–between model. The two imputation engines cover 24 specifications; the count stands for the rate, whose t and partial correlation are identical. Sources: `cases/eu-frames/data/menu_deviations.csv`, `cases/eu-frames/data/menu_options.csv`.")'
judgement_label <- c(other_question = "answers another question",
                     weaker_answer = "answers this question less well",
                     check = "a check of an answer on the eu_curve")
rule_kept <- c("wcr_rademacher", "re_cr1_g1", "rewb_cr2", "beta_cr1_g1", "mi_rubin_cr1_g1")
off <- devs |>
  filter(!on_curve, axis != "se", option != "rate", rule %in% rule_kept) |>
  left_join(eu_menu |> select(axis, option, label, judgement), by = c("axis", "option")) |>
  mutate(judgement = factor(judgement_label[judgement], judgement_label),
         label = reorder(label, below_zero_sig))
ggplot(off, aes(below_zero_sig, label, colour = judgement)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = below_sig(eu_curve), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = below_zero_sig, yend = label), linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0e3b6a", "#0f6b6b", "#8c5a10"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "below zero with p < 0.05", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Read against Auspurg, the pruning changes the picture in the direction that her reply to Ganslmeier and Vlandas leads one to expect. Of the specifications on the curve, `r pct_eu(below(eu_curve))` lie below zero and `r pct_eu(below_sig(eu_curve))` lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05. The options that answer other questions pull the share down furthest, pooled OLS to `r pct_eu(dv("estimator", "pooled_cl", "below_zero_sig"))` and the exclusion of the bailout countries to `r pct_eu(dv("sample", "no_bailout", "below_zero_sig"))`, while the options that answer the same question in another way stay close to the curve, among them the split rule for silent respondents at `r pct_eu(dv("noop", "split", "below_zero_sig"))`. The options that left the curve remain on the menu, the decision map and the class chart as material for reflection, each with its reason attached. That is a disclosure, and disclosure does not supply the justification that Auspurg demands; the justification lies in the reasons, which a reader can contest option by option.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Pick one decision of the [specification menu](../cases/eu-frames/menu.qmd) and write Auspurg's case for pruning it. Which of her four nonequivalence categories applies, and what would the curve look like if the decision were fixed at its best-justified option? Then write the case for keeping it, in Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman's terms: which purpose does varying this decision serve? The estimator and the sample are the two decisions where both cases are strong. Compare what you have written with the reason that the menu gives for each option.
:::

### 9.2 One correct analysis on a larger curve {#sec-eu-lakens}

The pruning described in section 9.1 moves some way towards the position of Lakens and colleagues. The inference rule of the curve, for instance, was decided from evidence about the data, the correlation of the residuals of a country from year to year and the few countries that carry most of the variation, rather than from convention, which is the kind of empirical work on an auxiliary assumption that they ask for. It stops short of their position on the estimator, where the curve keeps two designs because the claim, as written, does not say whether the changes common to all of Europe belong to the comparison, and their argument would require the analyst to settle that question before the test.

A participant choosing one specification from a fourteen-decision menu after ninety minutes of instruction is, on their reading, still choosing on an uninformed hunch. That limits what the exercise demonstrates without invalidating it.

### 9.3 The fork chart {#sec-eu-forks}

The fork chart of the EU-frames case decomposes the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlation across the `r nrow(eu_curve)` specifications of the curve by decision. The estimator carries `r pct_eu(fk("estimator"))`, the predictor `r pct_eu(fk("predictor"))`, the choice among the three positive scales `r pct_eu(fk("outcome"))` and the adjustment set `r pct_eu(fk("copredictor"))`, while the decisions of measurement together carry a few per cent and the interactions between decisions `r pct_eu(fk("interactions"))`. Moving the estimator alone changes whether a specification lies below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05 in `r pct_eu(fk("estimator", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs, and moving the predictor alone in `r pct_eu(fk("predictor", "crossing_rate"))`. Numbers like these invite a particular over-claim when they are put to the critics.

The over-claim would be that the dispersion on the curve is estimator dispersion rather than estimand dispersion, so that Auspurg's diagnosis no longer applies. The critics would reply that the estimator fork *is* an estimand fork in their sense, and on this curve the course agrees with them. Both designs that remain compare a country with itself over time, but the two-way design does so relative to the common European path of each year, while the design with country effects alone keeps the changes that every member state went through together, so that the two answer related but different questions, as the [statistical methods module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-two-designs) explains. The curve keeps both because both are defensible readings of the claim, and it names them as two estimands rather than presenting their spread as uncertainty about one quantity. The predictor is a fork of the same kind, since unemployment and GDP growth are two measures of 'poor national economic performance' between which the claim does not choose.

The decomposition supports a more modest reading, in which it *locates* where the argument has to happen. That use is endorsed by every party to the debate. Lakens and colleagues "support the use of multimodel analyses to hypothesize about 'which analytical decisions are most consequential'" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 6]; Ganslmeier and Vlandas offer their method as something that "can help inform which combinations of choices are more or less warranted" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 6]; Steegen and colleagues promised pointers to the most consequential choices from the start. Read this way, the fork chart identifies which decisions of the menu need a theory. A large estimator share means that you have to decide whether your question concerns change relative to the common European path or all change within a country, and a large predictor share means that you have to decide which measure of the economy the claim is about.

### 9.4 The strength of the evidence {#sec-eu-reading}

The rule of section 6 applies with more force to a larger curve. The share of the specifications of the EU-frames case that support its claim – `r pct_eu(below(eu_curve))` below zero on the curve of `r nrow(eu_curve)`, `r pct_eu(below_sig(eu_curve))` below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05 – is a description of a curated set of analyses, not the probability that the claim is true.

When the course quotes these shares, they describe the curve that you are looking at, and the [inference reading](../cases/eu-frames/reading-inference.qmd) exists to police the boundary between that description and any claim about evidence. For the permutation test designed in that reading, this means that a probabilistic device, the permutation p-value, is applied to an object that the current literature says should be read possibilistically. The reading explains what the test licenses under its sharp null, the hypothesis that the effect is zero in every unit, and this module adds a warning about everything that the test does not license.

Rohrer and colleagues also observe that a multiverse persuades only under a precondition: "This can only work if the results are fairly unambiguous across specifications" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 3]. On the curve of the claim the direction of the association meets that precondition, but the strength of the evidence does not, since whether a specification clears the 5% threshold depends mainly on the estimator: `r pct_eu(below_sig(country))` of the specifications with country effects alone lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05, against `r pct_eu(below_sig(twoway))` of the two-way ones, and the reproduced specification itself has a bootstrap p-value of `r num(eu_ref$p_wcr)`. The curve can therefore persuade a reader that the association runs in the direction of the claim within countries, and it leaves open whether the evidence is strong once the changes common to all of Europe are removed, which is a question about the estimand as much as about the data. The threshold itself carries its usual meaning here, because the bootstrap tests each specification against the variation of the countries, whose CR2 degrees of freedom (a median of `r num(median(eu_curve$df_cr2), 1)` across the curve) suggest that about a dozen of them effectively carry the information, rather than against the hundreds of thousands of respondents that make almost any coefficient significant in a respondent-level model. If you ever build a multiverse to defend a result of your own, this is the precondition to check before you lean on it.

The class chart of the EU-frames case is a many-analysts demonstration in the sense of section 6, with every declared specification, fixed in the Task 5 preregistration before it was run, drawn in black, and the specifications that were tried with `try_spec()` and submitted with `submit_exploration()` in Task 4 drawn in green. On this curve the class will not agree on the strength of the evidence, and it may not agree on the direction. Disagreement among the analysts in a class is no verdict on robustness in either direction, but it demonstrates that the dispersion documented by the many-analysts literature is real, reproducible and, once the menu and the preregistrations are on the table, *explainable*. The chart therefore serves reflection, practised as a group, and this is also the answer to anyone who asks why the class chart is allowed to straddle zero.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Open [the Multiverse page](../cases/eu-frames/multiverse.qmd) and find the black mark for the specification that you declared in Task 5 (or the reproduced specification, if you did not submit one). First read its neighbourhood possibilistically: what is the full range of aligned estimates among specifications that differ from yours on exactly one decision? Then catch yourself the moment you start counting – 'most of my neighbours agree with me' – and write one sentence on what that count would and would not establish, given how this universe was built.
:::

### 9.5 Heterogeneity and influence {#sec-heterogeneity}

The four sample restrictions of the EU-frames menu left the curve because each changes the population about which the claim is made, but the findings that they carry belong in the course, and three displays keep them. Each answers a question that a curve of one population cannot answer, namely where and when in that population the association is found, and none of them adds a point to the curve.

@fig-periods fits the 36 core specifications of the curve – the three positive scales on raw or logged unemployment or on growth, with or without the other measure of the economy, under both fixed-effects designs – on the full panel and on each half of it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-periods
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "The 36 core specifications of the curve on the full panel and on each half of it, by design. Open circles have bootstrap p < 0.05 and crosses p ≥ 0.05; the lines join the fits of one specification, and the burgundy line is the reproduced specification and its twin with country effects alone. The vertical axis is the claim-aligned partial correlation, so below zero is the direction of the claim. Source: `cases/eu-frames/data/display_periods.csv`."
per_plot <- periods |>
  mutate(design = factor(design_label[estimator], design_label),
         period = factor(sample, c("all", "y2004_2008", "y2009_2013"),
                         c("2004–2013", "2004–2008", "2009–2013")),
         p_class = if_else(p_wcr < 0.05, "p < 0.05", "p ≥ 0.05"),
         spec = paste(outcome, predictor, copredictor, pred_form),
         reproduced = is_ref_spec(periods))
ggplot(per_plot, aes(period, r_ca, group = spec)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(colour = "#0e3b6a", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = p_class), colour = "#0e3b6a", size = 2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = filter(per_plot, reproduced), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = filter(per_plot, reproduced), aes(shape = p_class),
             colour = "#8b1538", size = 2.4) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("p < 0.05" = 1, "p ≥ 0.05" = 4), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = minus) +
  facet_wrap(vars(design)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "claim-aligned partial r") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

For the reproduced specification the slope is `r num(per_ref("all", "b"), 5)` on the full panel (bootstrap p = `r num(per_ref("all", "p_wcr"))`), `r num(per_ref("y2004_2008", "b"), 5)` on 2004–2008 (p = `r num(per_ref("y2004_2008", "p_wcr"), 4)`) and `r num(per_ref("y2009_2013", "b"), 5)` on 2009–2013 (p = `r num(per_ref("y2009_2013", "p_wcr"))`), so that each half on its own gives a steeper slope than the panel as a whole, and among the 24 unemployment specifications `r pct_eu(below_sig(filter(per_unemp, sample == "all")))` lie below zero with bootstrap p < 0.05 on the full panel, `r pct_eu(below_sig(filter(per_unemp, sample == "y2004_2008")))` on 2004–2008 and `r pct_eu(below_sig(filter(per_unemp, sample == "y2009_2013")))` on 2009–2013. Neither half is a second answer to whether framing changed with the crisis. The earlier window contains no crisis, so its slope describes how framing tracked the smaller fluctuations of those years, and the later one drops the comparison with the years before the crisis and asks how framing moved with the deepening and easing of the crisis once it had begun. Read together, the two halves suggest that the association is not confined to the crisis years, and that it is somewhat stronger once the crisis had started.

@fig-loo leaves one country out at a time, from the reproduced specification and from its twin with country effects alone. The variation that identifies the two-way slope is concentrated in a few countries: once the fixed effects are removed, Greece holds `r pct_eu(vs("GR"))` of the variation in unemployment that is left, Spain `r pct_eu(vs("ES"))`, Poland `r pct_eu(vs("PL"))` and Ireland `r pct_eu(vs("IE"))`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-loo
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| fig-cap: "The slope of the cosmopolitan share on unemployment with one country left out at a time, under each design. Open circles have bootstrap p < 0.05 and crosses p ≥ 0.05; the burgundy line marks the slope on all 27 countries. Countries are ordered by the two-way slope without them. Source: `cases/eu-frames/data/display_loo.csv`."
country_order <- loo_two |>
  left_join(cnames, by = c("left_out" = "cntry")) |>
  arrange(desc(b)) |>
  pull(country)
loo_plot <- loo |>
  filter(left_out != "none") |>
  left_join(cnames, by = c("left_out" = "cntry")) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design_label[estimator], design_label),
         country = factor(country, country_order),
         p_class = if_else(p_wcr < 0.05, "p < 0.05", "p ≥ 0.05"))
loo_full <- loo |>
  filter(left_out == "none") |>
  mutate(design = factor(design_label[estimator], design_label))
ggplot(loo_plot, aes(b, country)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(data = loo_full, aes(xintercept = b), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = p_class), colour = "#0e3b6a", size = 2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("p < 0.05" = 1, "p ≥ 0.05" = 4), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = minus, n.breaks = 4) +
  facet_wrap(vars(design), scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "slope per point of unemployment, without the country", y = "country left out") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Leaving out one country moves the two-way slope between `r num(min(loo_two$b), 5)` (without `r cnames$country[cnames$cntry == loo_two$left_out[which.min(loo_two$b)]]`) and `r num(max(loo_two$b), 5)` (without `r cnames$country[cnames$cntry == loo_two$left_out[which.max(loo_two$b)]]`). None of the 27 two-way refits reaches bootstrap p < 0.05, as the full panel does not, while `r sum(loo_cty$p_wcr < 0.05)` of the 27 refits with country effects alone do. The display replaces a single hand-picked exclusion, such as leaving out Greece and Spain together, with the complete set, and its 27 refits are 27 checks of one answer rather than 27 answers.

@tbl-bailout fits the three positive scales on unemployment in the eight countries that received financial assistance and in the other nineteen separately, and tests the difference between the two groups in one model on all 270 cells. With eight clusters the Rademacher bootstrap can draw only 256 distinct sign patterns, so the table reads the Webb signs for the bailout countries.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bailout
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Slopes on unemployment in the eight bailout countries (Cyprus, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Portugal, Romania, Spain), in the other nineteen, and the difference between the two, estimated in one model on all 270 cells with an interaction. Bootstrap p-values in brackets, with Webb signs for the bailout countries and Rademacher signs otherwise. Source: `cases/eu-frames/data/display_bailout.csv`."
bailout |>
  filter(predictor == "unemp") |>
  mutate(p = if_else(group == "bailout", p_wcr_webb, p_wcr),
         cell = paste0(num(b, 5), " (", num(p), ")")) |>
  select(outcome, estimator, group, cell) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = cell) |>
  mutate(outcome = factor(outcome, c("mcosmo", "mutil", "mpos")),
         estimator = factor(estimator, names(design_label))) |>
  arrange(outcome, estimator) |>
  transmute(Scale = c(mcosmo = "cosmopolitan", mutil = "utilitarian",
                      mpos = "positive composite")[as.character(outcome)],
            Design = design_label[as.character(estimator)],
            `Bailout countries` = bailout, `Other countries` = other,
            Difference = difference) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(j = 3:5, align = "r") |>
  style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

For the reproduced specification the slope is `r num(ba("bailout", "b"), 5)` in the bailout countries (Webb p = `r num(ba("bailout", "p_wcr_webb"))`) and +`r num(ba("other", "b"), 5)` in the others (p = `r num(ba("other", "p_wcr"), 2)`), and the difference of `r num(ba("difference", "b"), 5)` has bootstrap p = `r num(ba("difference", "p_wcr"))`. The pattern holds for the cosmopolitan share and the positive composite under the two-way design, while the utilitarian scale does not share it.

Read together, the three displays suggest that the association between unemployment and positive framing is concentrated in the countries in which the crisis was deepest, and appears in both halves of the decade, which is what a reader of the claim needs to know about it. The reason for keeping them off the curve is the requirement of section 2. A curve that mixed the full panel with its halves and its subsets would count answers about different populations as votes on one question, and its share of supporting specifications would then depend on how many restrictions the menu happened to offer. As displays, the same fits show how the association varies across the population of the claim, which is a finding in its own right, without being read as evidence that the claim is robust or fragile.

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The debate read here: @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources and the reply by @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; @RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood with the companion post by @Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood; and @LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne. The origins: @SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience and @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis, with a framework for judging which analytic decisions are equivalent in @DelGiudiceGangestad2021TravelersGuideMultiverse. The many-analysts strand: @SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne, @BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers and @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, and, for the diagnosis that many disagreements between analysts are disagreements about the estimand, @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial. The book-length guide is @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, the tools are @SarmaEtAl2023MultiverseMultiplexingAlternative and @SarmaEtAl2024MilliwaysTamingMultiverses, and the classroom design is @HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom. Quotations from the PsyArXiv preprints are cited by the pagination of the preprints. The numbers on this page are computed when it is built from `spec_curve.csv`, `menu_options.csv`, `display_outcomes.csv`, `display_subgroups.csv` and `analysts5.csv` in `cases/housing/data/`, which are described by their codebooks. The numbers of section 9 are computed from files that the pipeline of the EU-frames case writes: the curve `cases/eu-frames/data/spec_curve.csv` and its decomposition `spec_curve_forks.csv`, the comparison of every option with its twins on the curve in `menu_deviations.csv`, the reasons in `menu_options.csv`, and the displays `display_periods.csv`, `display_loo.csv` and `display_bailout.csv`, which the [codebook of the displays](../cases/eu-frames/data/displays_codebook.md) describes.
